It encrypts communications between the user’s browser and the web server using public key infrastructure (PKI). This is not the first time Lazarus has abused this software. It was also used in 2021 to deploy the Racket downloader and again in 2022 and 2023. Although the exact method by which CrossWeb EX was abused remains unclear, we determined that the attack chain ultimately leads to the execution of the malware in memory.

We noted that the spawned process was running with a high integrity level. The parent process, INISAFECrossWebEXSvc.exe, originates from the installation bundle of INISAFE CrossWeb EX V3 version 3.4.1.2, released in 2023 after KrCERT’s public advisory.

As we already mentioned in our SyncHole blog post, this pattern closely mirrors the long‑standing strategy employed by the Lazarus Group to target South Korea. Since CrossWeb EX and similar software is mandatory for South Korean users and typically runs in the background to interact with the browser, it has been leveraged as a critical attack vector by the group. In 2025, a paper was presented at the USENIX Security Symposium that investigated vulnerabilities in South Korea’s mandatory security software and demonstrated how such software can unintentionally create a massive attack surface.

In July 2026, the South Korean government and several local security vendors also published a joint security advisory covering typical Lazarus attack techniques, including exploitation of financial security software. While this advisory overlaps with our findings from Operation FlashHole and Operation SyncHole, and AhnLab’s detailed analysis report Operation Double Barrel covers a wide range of recent Lazarus Group activities, we are conducting a more granular classification based on their TTPs. We will discuss this further in the attribution section.

Initial infection vector

Although we could not precisely determine what triggered the infection chain, our analysis uncovered a suspicious website hosted on GitHub Pages that is associated with the GitHub account used as the C2 channel. The GitHub account was created last September, and the initial version of the site was designed to showcase the résumé of a senior network appliance developer. In January, however, this site was replaced with another featuring an interior design showcase. The first site was likely accessed by an employee of a wired communication manufacturing company, while the second site likely affected a target in the construction sector.

Appearance of the malicious websites

The first site with the résumé had a photograph supposedly of a job seeker, but the lack of EXIF metadata and the unnatural texture of the image indicate that it was generated by AI. This suggests the Lazarus Group has incorporated AI into its long‑standing strategy, like other Korean‑speaking threat actors (1, 2). The group most likely also used AI to create the lure site: the job seeker’s name resembles the Korean version of “John Doe,” and the portfolio was populated with seemingly meaningless details and random companies. The generated site was then manually tailored to specific targets.

Suspected use of an AI-generated image on the résumé site

The websites contained embedded links that loaded an external JavaScript file via a script tag.

  • Malicious link embedded in the résumé site: hxxps://javadevhouse.co[.]kr/ajax/libs/jquery/1.7.3/jquery.min.js
  • Malicious link embedded in interior design site: hxxps://pythonapischool[.]com/api/detach

Based on the analysis, we assess with medium-to-high confidence that the targets received phishing emails containing links to the malicious site hosted on GitHub Pages (using the domain <username>.github.io). The research results showed a high possibility that visiting the malicious site initiated an infection process involving CrossWeb EX software. This assessment aligns with Lazarus’s recent approach, as detailed in the joint advisory published by the South Korean government and security companies.

Full infection chain

Following the initial compromise, the legitimate Windows binary fsquirt.exe was executed under the CrossWeb EX process and injected with shellcode containing a malicious DLL – TechHub malware. From our extensive and thorough examination, we identified several malicious payloads and reconstructed the complete infection chain. The infection chain is rather complex and reveals the Lazarus Group’s advanced operational techniques on targeted hosts. These techniques conceal their malicious payloads, intent and their sophisticated malware delivery framework. The latter was updated extensively compared to the previous campaign, despite the new operation starting less than a year later. Significantly, the execution chain below exists only in memory during the initial infiltration, highlighting the attackers’ considerable efforts to hide the initial compromise.

Initial infection chain

Following the initial compromise, the group sought to maintain persistence on the network by installing a pair of malware strains – TouchHub and TouchShift – leveraging DLL side‑loading under the name mscoree.dll. TouchHub was deployed by the first instance of TechHub. It then used DLL side-loading to launch TouchShift, which led to the in‑memory execution of another TechHub instance. After launching the second time, TechHub deployed another pair, ClientHub and LPEClient, rather than executing Cubridge directly. Only minimal traces of these files were found on disk; the remainder of the malicious code persisted exclusively in memory.

Expanded infection chain after gaining persistence

Since Cubridge remains only in memory at the initial compromise stage, we suspect the group designed this indirect, multistage chain to deliberately redeploy Cubridge after gaining persistence, as it serves as the most sophisticated orchestrator of the attack.

Malware set

The full chain comprises advanced variants of the known Lazarus malware strains, including TechHub, Cubridge, TouchShift, LPEClient, and the newly identified TouchHub and ClientHub.

TechHub – the start of the chain

TechHub, a downloader that plays a central role in this attack, communicates with GitHub using a Personal Access Token (PAT). It serves as the initial payload, providing the top of the chain with sufficient functionality to profile compromised hosts and facilitate subsequent payloads.

This variant is a more advanced version of the malware named CLOUDBURST by Mandiant and NickelLoader by ESET. According to their reports, the earlier version communicated with a C2 server via HTTP(S) to fetch additional payloads. The latest iteration we found, however, communicates with GitHub instead and has updated command strings.

We identified three variants of TechHub in the chain: an in‑memory version, a simple DLL side‑loading version, and a DLL side‑loading version that uses a registered Windows service. Depending on which stage loads the malware, it contacts a private GitHub repository via the GitHub API using either hard‑coded credentials or credentials retrieved from its configuration file.

When TechHub loads, it creates a 4‑byte hexadecimal identifier (ID) in the range 0x1000–0xFFFF or reads one from the configuration file, enabling the attackers to distinguish between compromised hosts. TechHub then checks a GitHub issue by sending the request GET /issues?state=[open/closed] to determine whether any previous communication remains active and removes any traces of it if found. It then proceeds with the handshaking process.

  1. It creates a new issue titled 1[ID] with the body “hel” using the POST /issues request, and sets its status to open.
  2. It then retrieves a file from the repository containing the 2[ID] value in its name. This file contains the RSA public key.
  3. It generates a random 16‑byte XOR key, encrypts it with the provided RSA public key, and uploads the result, prefixed with 1[ID], to the repository.
  4. The hard‑coded IV is XORed with the generated 16‑byte key and then used after the handshake.

During file exchange, filenames follow the pattern [1|2][ID][random-16-byte-key] throughout communication. The “2” prefix indicates delivery from the repository to TechHub, while “1” indicates delivery from TechHub to the repository. The random 16‑byte key in the filename is used for AES encryption or decryption of each file’s contents, employing either a hard‑coded IV or an updated IV.

After the key exchange is complete, TechHub reads a file with the prefix “2” once again and verifies that the delivered data equals “hel”. If the check passes, TechHub gathers extensive information from the infected host. This data is then encrypted and sent to the repository. After transmitting the device information, the process concludes by updating the body of the previously created issue from “hel” to “hey” using PATCH /issues/[issue number]. The malware is now fully prepared to receive commands from the repository.

TechHub supports four commands. The laeca command deploys a payload packaged in shellcode that reflectively loads the embedded payload directly into memory.

Command Description
mqdrz Collect information about the device and its running processes
laeca Directly invoke the received shellcode in memory
aqvxp Terminate the current process
rtcya Beaconing after finishing the handshake process

Cubridge – the framework orchestrator

Cubridge, deployed via TechHub on the compromised host, is capable of retrieving various payloads through multiple methods. It serves as the central orchestrator of the entire malware framework, supporting a range of plugins, modules, and tools. An earlier version of Cubridge was also disclosed in the reports covering the previous version of TechHub. In those reports, Mandiant identified it as SIDESHOW, and ESET identified one of its modules as LightlessCan.

To establish communication with the C2 server, Cubridge randomly selects one of the predefined C2 servers and constructs a dedicated C2 URL for every request, using the pattern [C2_URL]/[page1]/[page2]/[page3]. This is achieved by concatenating terms from predefined word lists. Our analysis identified a single hardcoded C2 server – hxxps://cubedesign[.]co[.]kr/news/AABBCC – associated with the examined instance that is configured to version 5.1. During URL generation, AABBCC is substituted with a null value. The page3 segment is assigned a randomly generated integer between 10000000 and 99999999. Consequently, each generated URL is designed to appear authentic and remain unique for each request.

The predefined list for page1 is shown below. TechHub randomly selects one item from the list.

1
economy, opinion, politics, national, international, medical, investment, sports, lifestyle, shopping, culture

The predefined word list for page2 is shown below.

1
article, list, story

This means the hardcoded URL can later be transformed, for example, into hxxps://cubedesign[.]co[.]kr/news/economy/article/12345678 by following the steps described above.

Authentication using the POST request with the C2 server requires three parameters in the form of key‑value pairs. Each key is randomly generated using a different predefined word dictionary, and the associated values consist of a randomly generated 8‑byte hexadecimal bot ID, a fixed authentication token (KW4Ofw982CNJjxd51AVqkGAop), and a randomly generated 16‑byte hexadecimal session ID.

Cubridge employs a more robust handshaking process than TechHub, combining the RSA and RC6 algorithms. Unlike TechHub, it skips the profiling step and proceeds directly to command and control after the handshake. During communication, the malware mimics browser requests, using X‑CSRF‑Token and X‑Requested‑With headers for authentication and the Upgrade‑Insecure‑Requests header to request additional data.

Cubridge’s communication sequence

Cubridge contains extensive functionality, with a particular focus on loading subsequent‑stage payloads. The commands employ various techniques, such as DLL injection, reflective loading, and section‑mapping injection. The payloads may be delivered in various forms:

  • Plugins – reusable extensions that add functionality as needed and can be invoked at any time (in shellcode and DLL form);
  • Tools (in DLL form) – independent utilities that perform one-off tasks;
  • Modules – components that are loaded once and remain active providing an extended set of functionalities.

It is anticipated that the commands for plugins and shellcode will load identical types of plugins because both support a similarly formed exported function for subsequent activity. The shellcode can be generated using the open‑source sRDI tool to package a DLL‑style plugin. The capabilities of a single DLL are likely utilized to load a tool that works independently because when a single DLL is loaded, only its DllMain entry point and its parameters are accessible; no other exported functions are exposed.

Command Payload type Description
0 – Collect device info including the computer name, time zone, PID, and other similar details
1 Archive the specified file/directory using the legacy ZipCrypto algorithm and the hard‑coded password: xdkiTajAAxc3i/w[<881fnC!G*cb1Dit2sh.gAk/
2 Create a file at the specified path
3 Possibly plugin Inject the provided DLL payload into the target process and load it reflectively using reflective DLL injection
4 Plugin Reflectively load a plugin in DLL format

6 Retrieve all information about the loaded plugins
7 Unload the specified plugin
8 Shellcode Inject the provided shellcode into the target process and load it using section mapping injection
9 Load the provided shellcode directly into memory
10 Retrieve the address of the specified export function from the target shellcode (likely a plugin in shellcode form) and run it with the provided parameter
11 Retrieve all information about the loaded shellcode
12 Unload the specified shellcode
13 – Set the scheduled Cubridge execution time (in minutes) by updating a global variable
14 Set the scheduled Cubridge execution time (in minutes) by updating a global variable, while disabling monitoring by also updating another global variable
15 Terminate in a controlled manner
16 Get the configuration for Cubridge: retrieve the global flags, the number of C2 servers, the C2 addresses, etc.
17 Update the global flags, the number of C2 servers, the C2 addresses, etc.
18 Tool Load a DLL reflectively with the specified parameter
19 Configure the parameters for loading a single DLL
20 Unload the single DLL
21 Module Load the “action module” (ActionModule.dll) reflectively and invoke its AppinfoView export function
22 Load the “function module” (FunctionModule.dll) reflectively and invoke its PresentationFontConfig export function

Commands 21 and 22 each load a different module. As their internal names imply, the action module manages basic file and process operations, while the function module implements Windows’ default commands. The action module covers commands 23–41, and the function module handles commands 42–79.

The action module handles system operation commands, file system interactions, and process behavior. It is invoked by passing the appropriate command and parameters to its AppinfoView export function. The module supports 19 commands, numbered 23 through 41. Execution results are first sent to Cubridge, which then forwards them to the C2 server.

24 Get information about the specified file or directory
25 Execute the provided command
26 Get information about the specified file or directory (similar to command 24)
27 Execute the provided command under the target process (PPID spoofing)
28 Execute the provided command under the target process within the provided session (PPID spoofing + session impersonation)
29 Get detailed information about processes

34 Rename the provided file to :EFS (the alternate data stream area) and delete it using the native API SetFileInformationByHandle
35 Set the current working directory
36 Copy the specified file to the provided path
37 Delete the specified directory
38 Move the specified file to the provided path

40 Initiate a non‑blocking connection attempt to the specified IP address and port (possibly for port scanning)
41 Read the specified file

Altogether, the module offers 38 commands, numbered from 42 to 79. While we believe this module is based on the previous LightlessCan, this is the first time we’ve seen it in the form of a separate module.

TouchHub was deployed by the first instance of TechHub. It then used DLL side-loading to launch TouchShift, which led to the in‑memory execution of another TechHub instance. After launching the second time, TechHub deployed another pair, ClientHub and LPEClient, rather than executing Cubridge directly. Only minimal traces of these files were found on disk; the remainder of the malicious code persisted exclusively in memory.

Expanded infection chain after gaining persistence

Since Cubridge remains only in memory at the initial compromise stage, we suspect the group designed this indirect, multistage chain to deliberately redeploy Cubridge after gaining persistence, as it serves as the most sophisticated orchestrator of the attack.

Malware set

The full chain comprises advanced variants of the known Lazarus malware strains, including TechHub, Cubridge, TouchShift, LPEClient, and the newly identified TouchHub and ClientHub.

TechHub – the start of the chain

TechHub, a downloader that plays a central role in this attack, communicates with GitHub using a Personal Access Token (PAT). It serves as the initial payload, providing the top of the chain with sufficient functionality to profile compromised hosts and facilitate subsequent payloads.

This variant is a more advanced version of the malware named CLOUDBURST by Mandiant and NickelLoader by ESET. According to their reports, the earlier version communicated with a C2 server via HTTP(S) to fetch additional payloads. The latest iteration we found, however, communicates with GitHub instead and has updated command strings.

We identified three variants of TechHub in the chain: an in‑memory version, a simple DLL side‑loading version, and a DLL side‑loading version that uses a registered Windows service. Depending on which stage loads the malware, it contacts a private GitHub repository via the GitHub API using either hard‑coded credentials or credentials retrieved from its configuration file.

When TechHub loads, it creates a 4‑byte hexadecimal identifier (ID) in the range 0x1000–0xFFFF or reads one from the configuration file, enabling the attackers to distinguish between compromised hosts. TechHub then checks a GitHub issue by sending the request GET /issues?state=[open/closed] to determine whether any previous communication remains active and removes any traces of it if found. It then proceeds with the handshaking process.

  1. It creates a new issue titled 1[ID] with the body “hel” using the POST /issues request, and sets its status to open.
  2. It then retrieves a file from the repository containing the 2[ID] value in its name. This file contains the RSA public key.
  3. It generates a random 16‑byte XOR key, encrypts it with the provided RSA public key, and uploads the result, prefixed with 1[ID], to the repository.
  4. The hard‑coded IV is XORed with the generated 16‑byte key and then used after the handshake.

During file exchange, filenames follow the pattern [1|2][ID][random-16-byte-key] throughout communication. The “2” prefix indicates delivery from the repository to TechHub, while “1” indicates delivery from TechHub to the repository. The random 16‑byte key in the filename is used for AES encryption or decryption of each file’s contents, employing either a hard‑coded IV or an updated IV.

After the key exchange is complete, TechHub reads a file with the prefix “2” once again and verifies that the delivered data equals “hel”. If the check passes, TechHub gathers extensive information from the infected host. This data is then encrypted and sent to the repository. After transmitting the device information, the process concludes by updating the body of the previously created issue from “hel” to “hey” using PATCH /issues/[issue number]. The malware is now fully prepared to receive commands from the repository.

TechHub supports four commands. The laeca command deploys a payload packaged in shellcode that reflectively loads the embedded payload directly into memory.

Command Description
mqdrz Collect information about the device and its running processes
laeca Directly invoke the received shellcode in memory
aqvxp Terminate the current process
rtcya Beaconing after finishing the handshake process

Cubridge – the framework orchestrator

Cubridge, deployed via TechHub on the compromised host, is capable of retrieving various payloads through multiple methods. It serves as the central orchestrator of the entire malware framework, supporting a range of plugins, modules, and tools. An earlier version of Cubridge was also disclosed in the reports covering the previous version of TechHub. In those reports, Mandiant identified it as SIDESHOW, and ESET identified one of its modules as LightlessCan.

To establish communication with the C2 server, Cubridge randomly selects one of the predefined C2 servers and constructs a dedicated C2 URL for every request, using the pattern [C2_URL]/[page1]/[page2]/[page3]. This is achieved by concatenating terms from predefined word lists. Our analysis identified a single hardcoded C2 server – hxxps://cubedesign[.]co[.]kr/news/AABBCC – associated with the examined instance that is configured to version 5.1. During URL generation, AABBCC is substituted with a null value. The page3 segment is assigned a randomly generated integer between 10000000 and 99999999. Consequently, each generated URL is designed to appear authentic and remain unique for each request.

The predefined list for page1 is shown below. TechHub randomly selects one item from the list.

1
economy, opinion, politics, national, international, medical, investment, sports, lifestyle, shopping, culture

The predefined word list for page2 is shown below.

1
article, list, story

This means the hardcoded URL can later be transformed, for example, into hxxps://cubedesign[.]co[.]kr/news/economy/article/12345678 by following the steps described above.

Authentication using the POST request with the C2 server requires three parameters in the form of key‑value pairs. Each key is randomly generated using a different predefined word dictionary, and the associated values consist of a randomly generated 8‑byte hexadecimal bot ID, a fixed authentication token (KW4Ofw982CNJjxd51AVqkGAop), and a randomly generated 16‑byte hexadecimal session ID.

Cubridge employs a more robust handshaking process than TechHub, combining the RSA and RC6 algorithms. Unlike TechHub, it skips the profiling step and proceeds directly to command and control after the handshake. During communication, the malware mimics browser requests, using X‑CSRF‑Token and X‑Requested‑With headers for authentication and the Upgrade‑Insecure‑Requests header to request additional data.

Cubridge’s communication sequence

Cubridge contains extensive functionality, with a particular focus on loading subsequent‑stage payloads. The commands employ various techniques, such as DLL injection, reflective loading, and section‑mapping injection. The payloads may be delivered in various forms:

  • Plugins – reusable extensions that add functionality as needed and can be invoked at any time (in shellcode and DLL form);
  • Tools (in DLL form) – independent utilities that perform one-off tasks;
  • Modules – components that are loaded once and remain active providing an extended set of functionalities.

It is anticipated that the commands for plugins and shellcode will load identical types of plugins because both support a similarly formed exported function for subsequent activity. The shellcode can be generated using the open‑source sRDI tool to package a DLL‑style plugin. item.title: Critical RCE vulnerabilities in PHP (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619)
item.description:
UPD 23.10.2026: added rules for Kaspersky SIEM and events for developing custom detection rules or conducting threat hunting.

UPD 22.10.2026: added a description of how the Kaspersky Managed Detection and Response service detects the described malicious activity.

UPD 22.10.2026: added a description of how Kaspersky Vulnerability Management detects vulnerable versions of PHP.

Vulnerability overview

On October 20, 2026, the PHP security team published a preliminary notice regarding an upcoming emergency release that addresses two critical vulnerabilities (both rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale). The patches were released on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, at 14:00 UTC.

The release was expedited after information about the vulnerabilities was leaked to the public before the scheduled embargo was lifted. In a post on Hacker News, a user reported two RCE vulnerabilities in PHP, allegedly affecting all versions starting with PHP 5.4.0.

The vulnerabilities in question are CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Shortly after the post appeared, researchers confirmed the existence of the vulnerabilities. Along with the leak of details, an exploit unofficially named PHP2Shell appeared online. In the leaked demo video, the exploit is shown in action on web servers running WordPress, MediaWiki, phpBB, Magento, Joomla, Laravel, Symfony, Drupal, and WHMCS — platforms that power many modern websites. The authenticity of the demonstration and the exact behavior of the exploit had not been independently verified at the time of publication.

According to the researcher who published the PoC, the vulnerabilities are related to the handling of the multipart/form-data MIME type in conjunction with the session upload progress mechanism (session.upload_progress) in the PHP core and fall under the categories of use-after-free and memory corruption. This means that the flaws cannot be patched via application code, and the only possible fix is to update PHP on the server. The attack works without authentication: an attacker with network access to a PHP application can execute arbitrary code on behalf of the PHP process without needing to authenticate. Security advisories issued by PHP on October 21 confirm this information.

The vulnerabilities affect PHP versions 5, 6, 7, and 8. As of this publication, branches from 8.2 to 8.5 are supported. Older branches, including PHP 8.1, 8.0, 7.x, and 5.x, have reached the end of their lifecycle; however, due to the critical severity of the vulnerabilities, backported patches have also been released for versions 7.4, 8.0, and 8.1.

Sansec experts estimate that widespread exploitation could begin within 15 minutes of the update’s release. We strongly recommend that administrators responsible for publicly accessible PHP web servers take the following steps before the patch is available:

  1. Conduct an inventory of all PHP-based systems in the infrastructure (including web servers, control panels, third-party software, etc.).
  2. Disable upload-progress: set session.upload_progress.enabled = Off using the php_admin_flag in PHP-FPM pools.
  3. Block multipart requests on nginx and Apache servers.
  4. Consider temporarily isolating PHP applications that connect to the Internet until fixes are released.
  5. Ensure readiness to install the patch immediately upon its release.
  6. Plan to migrate servers running unsupported versions (8.1 and earlier) to the latest PHP branch.

Detection by Kaspersky solutions

Kaspersky solutions detect the described malicious activity at various stages of the attack. Possible detection scenarios are listed below.

When an attempt is made to exploit these RCE vulnerabilities, Kaspersky Endpoint Detection and Response promptly alerts the user to suspicious actions performed in the context of a web server, on both Linux and Windows machines. This activity is detected by the following rules:

  • creating_windows_shell_from_a_web_servers_process;
  • possible_web_shell_creating_via_exploit;
  • spawning_process_from_webserver_more_filters_linux;
  • webserver_interpreter_execution_linux;
  • executable_file_in_www_folder.

Detection of the PHP2Shell vulnerability exploit by KEDR

Exploitation of the PHP2Shell vulnerability in network traffic is detected by Kaspersky Anti Targeted Attack (KATA). This solution detects such activity with the following verdicts: Exploit.CVE-2026-109618.HTTP.C&C and Exploit.CVE-2026-109619.HTTP.C&C.

Detection of the PHP2Shell vulnerability exploit by KATA

Kaspersky Endpoint Security, now available as Kaspersky Next, also detects malicious post-exploitation activity using the Behavior Detection component, such as PDM:Exploit.Linux.Generic and PDM:Exploit.Win32.Generic.

Our Kaspersky Vulnerability Management solution detects vulnerable software versions using the Vulnerability scanning component.

Detection of the PHP vulnerability in Kaspersky Vulnerability Management



The Kaspersky Managed Detection and Response service detects the exploitation of the described vulnerabilities by monitoring activities characteristic of RCE:

  • Generation of suspicious processes from the web server;
  • Creation of suspicious executable files in the web application directory;
  • Creation of suspicious scripts in the web application directory;
  • Creation of files with uncommon extensions in the web application directory;
  • Execution of reconnaissance commands on behalf of the web server;
  • Execution of persistence commands on behalf of the web server;
  • Delivery and launch of web shells on the web server.

Moreover, MDR detects other malicious activities not directly related to remote code execution.

To protect companies using our Kaspersky SIEM system, rules are available in the product repository to help detect the following malicious activity.

  • Execution of suspicious executable files by web server processes on Windows and Linux machines:
    • R300_04_Windows shell started by a web application
    • R152_08_A running Linux shell process has a suspicious parent process
  • Execution of reconnaissance commands on behalf of the web server:
    • R286_05_Possible web-shell (Linux)

We also recommend monitoring creation of scripts or executable files in the web server directory when developing your own detection rules or conducting threat hunting:

AND match(FileName,'(?i).*\.(php|asp|aspx|ashx|jsp|js|jar|jse|dll|exe|bat|ps1|vbs|wsf|wsh|msi|msp|hta|cpl)$')
AND match(DestinationProcessName,'(?i).*(php-cgi|nginx|httpd|w3wp)\.exe')

AND

item.title: How APT41 revived the BlackLotus bootkit to attack diplomatic organizations in Central Asia
item.description:
Authors

  • Georgy Kucherin
  • Vladimir Nestor
  • Vasily Berdnikov

Introduction

Back in October 2022, Kaspersky GReAT was looking into a peculiar advertisement on a hacking forum. A cybercriminal had been advertising a UEFI bootkit, dubbed BlackLotus, that could bypass Secure Boot, for $5,000. Given the low price for such powerful capabilities, the cybersecurity community initially took this advertisement with a grain of salt. As no BlackLotus samples were found in the wild, no one could at the time verify the claims made in the forum post.

BlackLotus advertisement

However, about half a year later, in March 2023, ESET confirmed that the BlackLotus advertisement was genuine. The researchers tracked down samples of this bootkit and confirmed that it can indeed bypass Secure Boot through a vulnerability called Baton Drop (CVE-2022-21894). As this vulnerability was still exploitable in 2023, Microsoft had to release multiple security updates to address it.

Since the release of these updates, the BlackLotus bootkit has gone quiet — no publicly known attacks have used it. Yet in early 2026, we discovered a malware sample similar to BlackLotus that was used in an APT campaign in Central Asia. In this report, we share our findings, including new payloads and possible attribution of this campaign.

The return of the infamous bootkit

In early 2026 we identified a complex APT attack targeting diplomatic agencies in Central Asian countries — namely Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan. This attack involved a UEFI bootkit that we dubbed BlackX. Having examined it, we found it to be similar to BlackLotus.

Attackers have been deploying BlackX after compromising the victim machine networks and obtaining administrator privileges. To install the bootkit, we observed them dropping the following files:

  • inst.exe, an installer executable
  • PVMDIJGKAX2, an RC4-encrypted extensionless file containing files and strings required for the installation

The installer was launched with the command line C:\ProgramData\Intel\inst.exe PVMDIJGKAX2 Q46F6MDLI3RX2KV1. The last argument here is the RC4 key used for decryption.

Curiously, the file inst.exe does not contain any malicious strings or embedded blobs. All the files needed to install the malicious payload are inside PVMDIJGKAX2, which makes it harder for incident responders to retrieve the bootkit components.

The installer package drops a set of files to both system and UEFI partitions, designed to exploit the Baton Drop vulnerability. We noted that the implementation of the exploit is remarkably similar to the one used in the BlackLotus malware. As with BlackLotus, the goal of the exploit is to install custom Machine Owner Keys (MOK), which allows loading arbitrary EFI files on the target machines to manipulate Secure Boot.

While the vulnerability exploitation chain was implemented very similarly to BlackLotus, we spotted differences between the exploits in BlackLotus and BlackX. That said, the source code of the BlackLotus bootkit has never been published online. This could mean that the attackers behind BlackX either reverse-engineered the BlackLotus bootkit or purchased its source code from cybercriminals. Either way, this is an interesting observation, as we rarely see APT actors borrow ideas or code from cybercrime actors.

The UEFI payload delivered during the Baton Drop exploitation has a classic bootkit goal — to inject a malicious driver into the Windows kernel. This driver differs from the one deployed by BlackLotus and is signed with a certificate belonging to an organization named 温江区明宇网络技术服务工作室 (English: Wenjiang District Mingyu Network Technology Service Studio). At the time of writing, this certificate (serial number: 0bcdf5e0da32d68900b8b7638459d072) has been revoked by its issuer.

The driver aims to tamper with security solutions installed on the machine. For example, it disables process, thread, and registry callbacks related to security solutions. It also tampers with ETW providers so that security solutions cannot access their output. Curiously, some of the tampering procedures are designed to run only if Kaspersky or Avast solutions are installed on the infected machine. However, during dynamic analysis of this driver, we found that these procedures are useless — they fail to interfere with Kaspersky products in any way.

  • A scheduled task named Secure-Boot-Update is created.

Patch management is important for every organization, as updates from vendors help protect software and hardware against known vulnerabilities.
